prompt: Put the layers a browser test passes through in order, from your test code down to the browser.
items: The runner, which finds and runs the test
The driver library, which turns `click()` into a message
The protocol, which carries the message
trap: The protocol is not a program you call; the library speaks it on your behalf.

prompt: A tester wants a tool that will test the shop in Safari. Why is a CDP-only library the wrong pick?

choices.text: CDP is too slow for a real browser
choices.why: Speed is not the limit; CDP talks straight to the browser with no driver in between.

choices.text: Only Chromium-based browsers speak CDP
choices.why: Right. CDP is Chrome's internal interface, so it reaches Chrome and Edge and stops there.

choices.text: CDP needs a separate driver program that Apple does not ship for its own browser
choices.why: That describes WebDriver, which has `safaridriver`; CDP has no driver at all.

choices.text: CDP cannot run headless, and Safari tests run headless
choices.why: Puppeteer runs headless over CDP by default; headless has nothing to do with Safari here.

prompt: What does a CDP connection give a library that a classic WebDriver connection does not?

choices.text: Events the browser sends without being asked, such as each response and console message
choices.why: Right. WebDriver is one request, one answer; CDP is a two-way WebSocket, which is how `look.mjs` printed the Network panel.

choices.text: Access to every browser
choices.why: The opposite: WebDriver reaches every browser with a driver, and CDP stops at Chromium.

choices.text: A W3C standard that does not change
choices.why: CDP is not a standard; it changes with Chrome. WebDriver is the standard.

choices.text: The ability to click
choices.why: Both click; the difference is what the browser can tell you on its own.

prompt: What does Puppeteer give you on its own, without anything else installed around it?

choices.text: A runner, assertions and a report
choices.why: Those come from a runner such as Jest; Puppeteer has none of them.

choices.text: A library that drives Chrome from a Node script
choices.why: Right. `basket.mjs` is a plain script; nothing in it is a test.

choices.text: A recorder that writes the script while you click
choices.why: Nothing was recorded; every line of `basket.mjs` was written by hand.

choices.text: A grid of browsers in the cloud
choices.why: Puppeteer starts one browser on your machine; grids belong to the WebDriver world of lesson 8.

prompt: Why does `basket.mjs` call `waitForSelector` before `page.click`?

choices.text: Because `page.click` throws if the button is not there yet, and the cards appear after the page loads
choices.why: Right. `app.js` draws the cards when `/api/products` answers, after `goto` has already returned.

choices.text: Because a selector must be registered before it is used
choices.why: Selectors are plain strings; nothing is registered.

choices.text: To make the browser draw the button
choices.why: Waiting draws nothing; the shop's script draws the cards, and the wait only notices when it has.

choices.text: To scroll the button into view
choices.why: `page.click` scrolls by itself; the wait is about the button existing.

prompt: A colleague's Puppeteer run printed `browser: Chrome/155.0.8059.39`; the transcript in this lesson printed Chrome 141. What explains the difference?

choices.text: The colleague has a newer Puppeteer than the one pinned
choices.why: Both use 25.13.0; that release is built for Chrome 155, which is the one it downloads.

choices.text: The colleague runs it with a window
choices.why: Headed or headless, the browser's version is the same.

choices.text: Version numbers differ on every run
choices.why: Timings differ between runs; a browser's version does not.

choices.text: Their install downloaded Puppeteer's own Chrome; the transcript pointed it at Playwright's Chromium
choices.why: Right. The machine the transcripts come from could not download, so `PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` named another browser.

prompt: In `tests/banana.spec.js`, which line does the job that `waitForFunction` did in the Puppeteer script?

choices.text: `await page.goto('/')`
choices.why: `goto` waits for the page to load, not for the count to change after a click.

choices.text: `await request.post('/api/reset')`
choices.why: That empties the basket before the test; it waits for nothing on the page.

choices.text: `await expect(page.getByTestId('basket-count')).toHaveText('1')`
choices.why: Right. The assertion keeps asking until the text is 1 or the timeout runs out.

choices.text: None: Playwright does not wait for the count
choices.why: It does, inside the assertion; that is why no wait is written by hand.

prompt: Which of these did Playwright add to what Puppeteer offers? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A test runner with fixtures and a report
choices.why: Right. Puppeteer leaves the runner to you.

choices.text: Assertions that retry until the page agrees
choices.why: Right. `toHaveText` waits; Puppeteer has no assertions at all.

choices.text: The ability to drive Chromium over CDP
choices.why: Puppeteer did that first; it is what both share.

choices.text: A `page.locator()` method that waits before acting
choices.why: The Puppeteer you installed has one too; the difference left is the waiting assertion and the runner.

prompt: A page redraws its product cards every few seconds. Why does a Playwright locator cope with that better than a Puppeteer element handle fetched once?

choices.text: A locator caches the element so it never goes stale
choices.why: It does the opposite: it keeps no element and searches again each time.

choices.text: A locator is a description searched for again on every use
choices.why: Right. A handle points at the old card; the locator finds whichever card is there now.

choices.text: Playwright stops the page from redrawing during a test
choices.why: It changes nothing about the page; tests see the page as it behaves.

choices.text: Locators only use test ids, which survive a redraw
choices.why: The test also found the button by its role and name; what matters is the repeated search.

prompt: A team has two hundred tests on a WebDriver grid and wants to listen to the page's network requests as well. Which tool fits without leaving WebDriver behind?

choices.text: Puppeteer, because it sees the network through CDP
choices.why: It would leave the grid behind: Puppeteer does not speak classic WebDriver.

choices.text: Jest, because it has a watch mode
choices.why: Jest drives no browser; the watch mode reruns tests when files change.

choices.text: WebdriverIO, which moves to WebDriver BiDi where the browser supports it
choices.why: Right. BiDi keeps WebDriver's reach and adds the events CDP is known for.

choices.text: Nightwatch, because it is made by a cloud company
choices.why: Who makes it says nothing about events; Nightwatch sits on `selenium-webdriver` and classic WebDriver.

prompt: What is underneath Nightwatch when it talks to a browser?

choices.text: Puppeteer
choices.why: Puppeteer is a CDP library; Nightwatch depends on Selenium's.

choices.text: `selenium-webdriver`, so classic WebDriver
choices.why: Right. Nightwatch 3.16.0 depends on `selenium-webdriver` 4.27.0.

choices.text: A protocol of its own
choices.why: Its README says it uses the W3C WebDriver API.

choices.text: Jasmine
choices.why: Jasmine is a framework for writing tests; it talks to no browser.

prompt: WebdriverIO opts in to the two-way protocol by itself; the capability `wdio:enforceWebDriverClassic` keeps it on plain WebDriver instead of WebDriver ___ .
hint: The name says the connection goes both ways.

prompt: Without any other package, what can Jest do to the shop's page in a browser?

choices.text: Open it in Chromium
choices.why: Jest has no driver library; it cannot open a browser.

choices.text: Nothing: Jest drives no browser by itself
choices.why: Right. A browser arrives only with a library such as Puppeteer, for instance through `jest-puppeteer`.

choices.text: Click its buttons through jsdom, the same as a browser would
choices.why: jsdom is not the shop's page in a browser: it has no layout, and the page's own server is not involved.

choices.text: Record a video of it
choices.why: Video belongs to browser runners; lesson 16 covers it in Playwright.

prompt: A jsdom test clicks the basket's button and passes, yet on a 360-pixel phone the button is pushed off-screen by lesson 7's wide basket. Why did the test not notice?

choices.text: The test should have waited for the button
choices.why: Waiting would not help: the button was there and clickable in jsdom.

choices.text: Jest runs tests in parallel and missed it
choices.why: Parallelism has nothing to do with it; a single test would pass the same way.

choices.text: jsdom has no layout, so nothing in it has a size or a position
choices.why: Right. Overflow is a layout fact, and only a real browser computes it.

choices.text: The test used a CSS selector instead of a role
choices.why: A role would have found the same button; neither sees where it is drawn.

prompt: Why does a simple Jasmine spec usually run in Jest unchanged?

choices.text: Both call the same browser driver
choices.why: Neither calls a browser driver at all.

choices.text: Jest began by running on Jasmine and kept its syntax
choices.why: Right. `describe`, `it` and `expect(...).toBe(...)` came across with it.

choices.text: Both are made by the same company
choices.why: Jest came out of Facebook; Jasmine is a separate project.

choices.text: A W3C standard defines `describe` and `it`
choices.why: The W3C standardises WebDriver, not test syntax.

prompt: Match each tool to the kind of thing it is.

pairs.right: A service that writes and runs your tests

prompt: What does a team give up when an outside service writes and runs its end-to-end tests?

choices.text: The ability to run Playwright at all
choices.why: The tests are Playwright code; nothing stops the team running Playwright itself.

choices.text: Knowing, inside the team, what is tested and why
choices.why: Right. That knowledge decides where testing effort goes, and it now lives with somebody else.

choices.text: Its unit tests, which the service replaces
choices.why: The service writes end-to-end tests; unit tests stay where they were.

choices.text: Access to browsers other than Chrome
choices.why: Which browsers are covered is a question about Playwright and the contract, not about outsourcing as such.

prompt: A Python team whose testers do not program is asked to automate the shop's acceptance tests. By the lesson's order of questions, which choice fits first?

choices.text: Puppeteer inside Jest
choices.why: Both are JavaScript and both need a programmer; the team is Python and its testers do not program.

choices.text: Robot Framework with the Browser or Selenium library
choices.why: Right. It is Python, and keywords are written by people who are not programmers.

choices.text: Nightwatch, for its configuration wizard
choices.why: A wizard does not write the tests; they would still be JavaScript.

choices.text: WebdriverIO, for WebDriver BiDi
choices.why: A protocol feature answers none of the team's first questions: language and who writes the tests.

prompt: A team's suite must cover Chrome, Firefox and Safari, and its unit tests live in Jest. A developer proposes Puppeteer inside Jest for the browser tests. What is the strongest objection?

choices.text: Puppeteer cannot run inside Jest
choices.why: It can; `jest-puppeteer` does exactly that.

choices.text: Jest is too slow for browser tests
choices.why: The runner's speed is not what fails here; the browsers are.

choices.text: Puppeteer reaches Chrome and Firefox but not Safari
choices.why: Right. CDP stops at Chromium and Puppeteer's BiDi covers Firefox; Safari needs WebDriver or Playwright's WebKit.

choices.text: Puppeteer has no way to click by role
choices.why: Its selectors can query by role and name; the reach of its protocols is the problem.

prompt: Which of these is a hosted service rather than software you install?

choices.text: WebdriverIO
choices.why: It is an npm package: a library and a runner.

choices.text: Robot Framework
choices.why: It is a Python package you install with pip.

choices.text: Jasmine
choices.why: It is an npm package that runs specs.

choices.text: QA Wolf
choices.why: Right. Its npm package is deprecated; what it sells is people writing and running tests.
